- Seigaiha is a traditional Japanese pattern of overlapping waves. Its waves stretch endlessly across the design, carrying a wish for a peaceful life that continues into the future. The 15oz selvedge denim is slowly woven on old shuttle looms with indigo on both sides. Strongly slubbed, rope-dyed indigo yarn forms the warp, while a finer, deeper indigo yarn forms the weft. Coin-shaped copper rivets, Shogyomujo pocket bags and a specially designed deerskin patch add the familiar Samurai details. As the denim changes with wear, the small red sun remains a reminder of the idea that began it all.

A roomy 1940s-inspired silhouette meets Samurai’s distinctive 15oz Seigaiha selvedge denim. Woven from Texas cotton with indigo yarns in both the warp and weft, this fabric combines pronounced slub with a depth of colour that develops gradually through wear. One-washed and made in Japan.

FIT & SIZING

The S3000 draws on Samurai’s S3000VXII wartime-inspired pattern, with a mid-to-high rise, generous thigh and wide straight leg. Minimal taper preserves the relaxed proportions from the hip through to the hem.

This model runs slightly small, with the waist measuring just below the tagged size. We recommend sizing up one from your usual size in most American denim brands to maintain the intended fit. SEIGAIHA: BLUE OCEAN WAVES

Named after the traditional Japanese seigaiha wave pattern, this denim takes its inspiration from the repeating arcs seen on textiles and ceramics. The motif represents calm seas and a wish for lasting peace.

Samurai carries this theme into the finishing details. A red-painted “hinode” top button evokes the sunrise over the sea, while the jacquard pocket lining features “shogyo mujo” (諸行無常), a Buddhist expression referring to the impermanence of all things—a fitting detail for denim that continually changes with its wearer.

The fabric’s character comes from the contrast between its two yarns: a heavily slubbed #5 rope-dyed indigo warp and a finer #8 indigo weft, dyed to a darker shade using a different method.

Initially, the textured warp gives the denim its dominant blue tone and uneven surface. As the yarns fade at different rates, the darker weft becomes more visible, adding depth to the developing fades.

Woven slowly on vintage shuttle looms, the 15oz fabric offers substantial texture in a weight suited to regular wear. Both warp and weft are dyed with indigo.

product.body_html:
The Studio D’Artisan SD-1001E takes one of the brand’s most recognisable straight-leg patterns and gives it an entirely different character through its remarkable 15oz GL3 ecru selvedge denim.

Instead of relying on indigo dye, the yarns are left in their natural, warm ecru/kinari tone, allowing the construction and texture of the denim to take centre stage. The result is a fabric with a dry, earthy appearance and an exceptionally tactile surface—far removed from the smooth, uniform character of modern mass-produced denim.

Woven on a piece of Japanese denim history

The real story behind the SD-1001E is its GL3 denim.

Studio D’Artisan develops this fabric specifically around the characteristics of the vintage Toyoda GL3 shuttle loom, a machine dating back more than half a century. The loom is exceptionally slow by modern standards, producing only around five metres of fabric per hour, and maintaining these machines is itself a painstaking process because replacement parts are no longer readily available.

That inefficiency is precisely what makes the resulting denim so interesting.

Rather than producing a perfectly consistent surface, the GL3 creates natural variation throughout the cloth. Studio D’Artisan further tunes the yarn texture, yarn count and weave construction to emphasise those characteristics, producing pronounced slub, irregularity and depth that contemporary high-speed looms struggle to reproduce.

The fabric therefore feels alive: uneven, rugged and slightly unpredictable, with subtle changes in texture visible across the entire pair.

Natural ecru rather than indigo

The Ecru designation is more than simply a colour choice.

Because the yarns are not indigo-dyed, the denim retains the natural colour of the cotton yarn itself. This gives the SD-1001E a softer, warmer starting point than traditional blue selvedge and allows its evolution to take a different path as it is worn.

The neutral tone also makes the jeans unusually versatile. They work naturally with faded workwear, military pieces, knitwear, overshirts and simple everyday clothing, while the heavily textured denim gives even a minimal outfit plenty of visual interest.

The classic Studio D’Artisan straight fit

The SD-1001E uses Studio D’Artisan's classic regular straight silhouette, based on the brand's traditional SD-1000 series pattern.

It has a comfortable mid-to-slightly-higher rise, a generous top block and a full straight leg from the thigh through to the hem. It is relaxed without becoming oversized and structured without feeling restrictive.

The result is a timeless fit that works particularly well with boots, sneakers and heritage footwear.

Details made for long-term wear

The construction follows the traditional five-pocket jean format and includes a button fly, copper hardware, leather patch and selvedge detailing. The pocket construction and off-centre belt-loop placement add further touches of Studio D’Artisan's distinctive approach to classic denim design.

The denim is 100% cotton, 15oz and Made in Japan. This particular version is offered in a one-washed/rinsed state by retailers, making it considerably easier to wear from the beginning while retaining the substantial character of the GL3 fabric.

Why the SD-1001E stands out

The appeal of the SD-1001E isn't about making another pair of ecru jeans.

It is about combining old Japanese weaving technology, deliberately irregular yarn, a substantial 15oz weight and an undyed natural colour into a jean that changes the way you experience selvedge denim.

The surface is rugged.
The colour is understated.
The fit is classic.
And the fabric has the kind of irregular character that can only come from a slow, traditional weaving process.

For anyone looking beyond perfectly clean, modern denim, the SD-1001E GL3 offers something much more tactile and authentic: a pair of Japanese selvedge jeans where the imperfections are part of the design—and where the natural ecru fabric gives the familiar Studio D’Artisan silhouette an entirely new personality.

product.title: STUDIO D'ARTISAN "D4620" GL3 DENIM COVERALL
product.body_html:
The Studio D’Artisan D4620 GL3 Denim Coverall is built around one of the most characterful fabrics in Japanese denim: heavyweight 15oz denim woven slowly on a vintage Toyoda Automatic Loom Works GL3 shuttle loom.

Originally developed around half a century ago, the GL3 represents an early generation of Japanese power looms. Today, keeping these machines running is an involved process. Replacement parts are no longer readily available, meaning worn components often have to be salvaged from other retired GL3 machines. Even by vintage shuttle-loom standards, production is remarkably slow, with the loom capable of weaving only around 5 meters of fabric per hour.

That inefficiency is precisely what makes the resulting denim so special.

Rather than producing the perfectly uniform surface associated with modern high-speed weaving, the GL3 creates a fabric full of irregularity, slub, texture and natural variation. The finished denim has the rugged, uneven character associated with workwear denim from generations ago — a depth and roughness that is extremely difficult to reproduce with modern machinery.

For the GL3 Series, Studio D’Artisan went further than simply putting denim through an old loom. The brand developed its own carefully calibrated recipe, experimenting with the texture and count of the yarns, the shade of the rope-dyed indigo, and the warp and weft density. Numerous test weavings were carried out before arriving at the final fabric.

The result is a 15oz GL3 selvedge denim with a distinctly vintage hand and pronounced surface character. The unevenness is intentional: every slub, irregularity and subtle variation contributes to the personality of the cloth. The denim is designed to develop further with wear, rewarding the owner with increasingly individual fading and character over time.

The D4620 itself takes the form of a classic denim coverall, drawing directly from traditional workwear while avoiding a boxy or overly utilitarian appearance. Its gently flared A-line silhouette gives the jacket a distinctive shape, combining the practicality of a traditional chore coat with a more refined contemporary profile.

Details reinforce its workwear roots, including large utility pockets, original Studio D’Artisan metal hardware, selvedge detailing and a leather neck patch. The jacket is constructed from 100% cotton and is available in a one-wash finish, making it easier to wear from the outset while retaining the substantial character of the GL3 cloth.

This is not simply a coverall made from heavyweight denim. It is a jacket built around a piece of textile history — a fabric that can only exist because an increasingly rare vintage loom is still being kept alive.

Rather than reproducing a single historical garment, this pair blends factual references with imaginative interpretation — a denim “what if?” rooted in military and workwear history.

During World War II, strict government regulations reshaped everyday clothing. Denim production was forced to adapt: surplus fabrics were reused, trims were simplified, and non-essential details were removed to conserve materials. Many skilled craftsmen were reassigned to military uniform production, leaving jeans to be sewn by less-experienced workers. The result was denim with rough stitching, uneven details, and a utilitarian character born of necessity rather than design.

Studio D’Artisan takes this historical context and projects it forward into the Vietnam War era. The brand imagines how denim might have continued to evolve under similar constraints — becoming even more stripped-back, functional, and raw. The result is a pair of jeans that feels authentic, rugged, and intentionally imperfect.

Key design elements reflect this concept. The back pocket stitching is painted rather than sewn, echoing material-saving techniques. The pocket bags feature tiger stripe camouflage, a pattern widely used during the Vietnam War. Iron laurel buttons, an era-inspired tear-away style label, and detailing based on the classic 1966 denim model further reinforce the historical narrative.

Despite its utilitarian inspiration, the jean maintains balance and wearability. The classic straight silhouette offers a timeless fit, while the 14oz original selvedge denim provides durability with character. Finished with oxidized Studio D’Artisan buttons, engraved copper rivets, selvedge construction throughout, and a recycled paper pulp waistband patch, every detail feels deliberate and story-driven.

This is not a reproduction — it’s a reinterpretation. A piece that merges history, imagination, and craftsmanship, celebrating the beauty found in imperfection and the enduring appeal of wartime denim aesthetics.

This patch symbolizes the artistry, tradition, and collaboration between skilled artisans, embodying the quality Graph Zero is known for. The engraving reads: "THE ONE AND ONLY TEXTILE" and "JAPAN PRIDE," a proud statement of the brand’s heritage and dedication.

Graph Zero’s Heritage Jeans are designed to stand out, even when worn oversized. For a touch of timeless style, pair them with suspenders and embrace a classic, vintage aesthetic.

The NOLITA Frog Skin Camo Overshirt is our Brooklyn take on a piece of military history. Frog skin — the iconic WWII-era camouflage pattern worn by the first Marine Raiders — gets reinterpreted here in a 10oz Japanese back satin: a tightly woven 100% cotton fabric with a smooth face, subtle sheen, and the kind of structured hand that softens beautifully with wear.

In 1942, a garden editor at Better Homes and Gardens designed the first camouflage pattern in American military history. Norvell Gillespie, a horticulturist by training, looked to nature — the mottled skin of a frog, the way light breaks through a forest canopy — and created a five-color disruptive pattern that would become known as frog skin.

The Marine Raiders wore it first, landing on Tulagi in the Solomon Islands in the dark early hours of August 6, 1942. It went on to see action at Guadalcanal and Bougainville, briefly appeared at Normandy before being pulled back — it looked too much like SS camouflage and was causing friendly fire — and eventually made its way into surplus stores, then hunting gear, then street culture. The CIA issued it to Cuban exiles for the Bay of Pigs. Special Forces gave it to the Montagnard in Vietnam. It's one of the most traveled patterns in the history of American cloth.

product.title: NAVY YARD Sashiko Chore Coat
product.body_html:
Note: Indigo transfer can occur with sashiko fabric and will decrease and stop with wear. Avoid white surfaces while breaking in. 

The NAVY YARD Sashiko Chore Coat is our Brooklyn take on one of the oldest garments in the working world. It combines two of our all time favorite things: sashiko fabric — a Japanese stitching technique that became a fabric, dating back centuries — meets the chore coat, a silhouette born in 19th century France and worn by laborers on both sides of the Atlantic ever since.

The result is a 16oz coat built to last decades, rinsed once to remove shrinkage but preserves the deep indigo color that will fade beautifully with time and wear. Real horn buttons. Triple-stitched seams. Hidden interior pockets. Made at 108 Bayard Street, Williamsburg, Brooklyn — a couple miles from the Navy Yard.

The chore coat begins in France, around 1844. A garment for railway workers, farmers, and factory laborers — built from cotton drill or moleskin, dyed with a benzoate-based blue that would hide the stains of manual labor. They called it the bleu de travail. "Blue work." The term "blue collar" follows from the same cloth.

By the 1920s, Carhartt had brought it to America with triple-stitched seams, riveted pockets, and a corduroy collar. Paul Newman wore one in Cool Hand Luke. Tupac wore one to the Soul Train Awards in 1993. Bill Cunningham rode his bike around New York City in one well into his 80s. It has appeared on the runways of Valentino, Balenciaga, and Prada without ever fundamentally changing what it is: a boxy cut, patch pockets, a button front, and cloth tough enough to outlast the person wearing it.

In Japan, a parallel tradition was developing — the noragi, a loose indigo jacket worn by farmers and artisans, reinforced with sashiko stitching to extend the life of the garment through hard use. The techniques are different. The philosophy is identical.

product.title: OG 718 Fatigue Pant (Olive)
product.body_html:

The OG 718 Fatigue Pant is our modern interpretation of the historic fatigue pants worn by the U.S. military from the 1950s through the 1970s, including the Korean and Vietnam War eras. We studied original references closely, then refined the design with contemporary updates that elevate both function and feel.

Constructed from a 10oz Japanese back satin fabric, this cloth features a soft yet durable structure, woven with American cotton and milled in Japan. The fabric offers a balance of comfort and resilience, designed to break in naturally over time while maintaining its integrity.

Design details include pure brass snap buttons at the waistband tabs and leg openings, along with considered pocket construction. The front andrear cargo pockets are tacked down to create clean lines while still allowing for practical storage and ease of movement.

The OG 718 name is a nod to both the original OG-107 military style and Brooklyn’s 718 area code — bridging heritage and home. This piece is built to diversify a wardrobe, offering an alternative to denim while maintaining the same level of depth and character. The result is a pant that feels rooted in tradition but entirely relevant today.
